word_study.significance: This is not a simple statement of how much Haman owns but a claim about the honor and status that his wealth conveys. Kevod emphasizes that his riches are not private — they are visible, they are a source of glory, they are part of how he is seen in the world.

word_study.meaning: The abundance, multitude, or great number of his children. Rov refers to abundance or magnitude; banav means 'his sons'.
word_study.significance: In ancient Near Eastern context, many sons were a mark of divine blessing, prosperity, and security for the future. Haman boasts of his sons as evidence of his favor and power. (This makes later references to Haman's sons — particularly their execution in Esther 9 — all the more painful.)

word_study.meaning: Made him great / elevated him, lifted him up. Gadal means 'to make great'; nasa' means 'to lift up, to elevate, to exalt'.
word_study.significance: Both verbs emphasize the king as the agent of Haman's elevation. Haman is not claiming to be inherently great; he is claiming that the king made him great. This is why his dependence on the king's favor is so absolute — without the king's will, he has no status.

word_study.meaning: The officials/princes and servants/slaves. Sarim are high officials; avdim are lower servants or subjects.
word_study.significance: By claiming elevation 'above' both categories, Haman is claiming to stand alone at the top of the hierarchy below the king. He is not simply honored — he is uniquely honored, elevated above even his peers.

cross_references.connection: Job's explicit rejection of trusting in gold or rejoicing in riches — a direct counterpoint to Haman's boasting about his wealth.

'Be not thou afraid when one is made rich, when the glory of his house is increased; for when he dieth he shall carry nothing away: his glory shall not descend after him.' — A direct biblical comment on the futility of Haman's boasting.
'The rich man's wealth is his strong city' — Haman believes his wealth and status are his security, unaware that they will not protect him.
The parable of the rich fool, who boasts of his abundance and plans for the future, only to be required to account for his soul that very night — a direct parallel to Haman's situation.
The execution of Haman's ten sons, turning his boast about the 'multitude of his children' into a grief that transforms the meaning of this verse retroactively.

commentary.historical_context: In Persian court culture, the display of wealth and the enumeration of honors was a standard form of social communication. A man's status was literally visible in his possessions, his attendants, his titles, and his family. Haman's boasting would not have seemed out of place in the context of the Persian court — it was a normal and expected way of asserting one's position. However, biblical wisdom literature consistently warned against this kind of boasting as spiritually dangerous. The Hebrew scriptures emphasized that all blessings come from the Lord and that trust in earthly riches and honors was foolish.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Korihor's boasting about his sophistication and rejection of faith (Alma 30:31) parallels Haman's catalog of self-glorification. Both men have confused worldly honor with actual power and lack the spiritual perception to see their vulnerability.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 78:6 teaches that 'it is more blessed to give than to receive' — Haman's entire monologue is about receiving and possessing. The Doctrine and Covenants consistently warns against the pride that comes from imagining that one's increase is due to one's own power or wisdom.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant explicitly rejects the pride of worldly status. In the endowment narrative, candidates are called to approach God stripped of the symbols of worldly rank and honor. Haman's boasting about his elevation and status represents the spiritual posture that the temple explicitly rejects.

commentary.christological_typology: Haman's catalog of self-glorification contrasts sharply with Christ's emptying of himself (Philippians 2:7) and his rejection of earthly honor (John 5:41). Where Haman finds identity in accumulation and recognition, Christ found identity in obedience and service.
commentary.application: This verse invites ruthless self-examination: What do we boast about? What accomplishments, possessions, or honors do we catalog when we want others to recognize our importance? Do we credit God in those moments, or do we take the credit ourselves? The most dangerous boasting is the kind we don't recognize as boasting — the casual way we highlight our children's achievements, our professional success, our possessions. Haman's boasting is not obviously evil; it is simply a catalog of facts. But the lack of gratitude, the absence of any acknowledgment that these things could be lost, the complete centering of identity on accumulation — these are the spiritual red flags. We are vulnerable to Haman's fate whenever we believe that our status, our wealth, or our accomplishments are the foundation of our security.

text_kjv: Haman said moreover, Yea, Esther the queen did let no man come in with the king unto the banquet that she had prepared but myself; and to morrow am I invited unto her also with the king.

commentary.narrative:
Haman moves from boasting about his possessions and titles to boasting about his exclusive social access — and this, to him, is the crowning achievement. The emphatic 'af' ('moreover, indeed') introduces what he considers his supreme glory: 'Queen Esther invited no one but me to come with the king to the banquet she prepared.' This is not a public honor that anyone can witness; it is a private, intimate recognition. And it is all the more precious to Haman because it comes from the queen, a woman, and because it is exclusive — 'no one but me.'

Then comes the final detail of his boasting: 'And tomorrow too I am invited by her, along with the king.' He has been invited a second time. Not only does the queen honor him uniquely once, but she has committed to doing so again. Haman hears in this a deepening favor, a sign that his position is not just high but secure. What he cannot see — what the reader knows because Esther has explicitly told the king in verse 8 that she will reveal her request tomorrow — is that Esther has invited him to the exact banquet where his destruction will be announced. Haman's exclusive access to the queen is the rope he is weaving for his own hanging. The irony is profound: the very thing he boasts about as his greatest security is the mechanism of his undoing.

word_study.meaning: Also, moreover, indeed, even. The particle af can mean 'even' or 'also' and often introduces an additional or emphatic point.
word_study.significance: Af signals that Haman is moving to what he considers an even greater achievement than his wealth and titles. This is his emotional climax — the moment where his boasting peaks.

word_study.meaning: Called, invited, summoned. The passive form qaru'a indicates that Haman has been called or summoned by the queen.
word_study.significance: The passive form emphasizes that this honor is bestowed on Haman by Esther — he is the object of her invitation, which makes the honor even more precious to him because it is her choice to elevate him.

word_study.meaning: Not, no. The negative particle that creates absolute denial.
word_study.significance: The absolute nature of Haman's exclusivity — 'no one but me' — is what makes this honor, in his mind, supreme. It is not merely that he was invited; it is that he was the only one invited. The exclusivity is the entire point.

word_study.meaning: 'Also for tomorrow' or 'tomorrow too.' Gam means 'also'; machar means 'tomorrow.'
word_study.significance: The word 'also' (gam) suggests repetition and continuation of favor. Haman hears in this a pattern of increasing honor — if he is invited a second time, perhaps a third invitation will follow. He is imagining a future of deepening access and influence.

cross_references.connection: The second banquet where Esther will reveal her petition, and Haman's exclusive invitation will become the context of his destruction.
After Haman's death, the king will give Haman's house to Esther — the very queen who invited him to his doom now receives his possessions.
'Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall' — Haman's boasting about his exclusive access is the pride that immediately precedes his fall.

The prophecy against Babylon: 'Now therefore hear this, thou that art given to pleasures... I am, and none else beside me; I shall not sit as a widow... these two things shall come to thee in a moment in one day.' — A direct parallel to Haman's sense of unique security and the sudden reversal.

commentary.historical_context: Private banquets with the royal couple were the ultimate form of social access in the Persian court. To be invited to such an occasion was extraordinarily rare and signified extraordinary favor. For a man to be the only non-royal guest invited to such a banquet was a mark of supreme honor. Haman's excitement about being invited a second time suggests he understands the significance of what has happened — he has crossed into the innermost circle of the court's social hierarchy. The fact that the invitation came from the queen (not the king) is also significant — it suggests an independent choice by Esther and implies that she values Haman personally. He cannot imagine that this is a strategic deception.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: King Noah's confidence in his position at the court (Mosiah 11) parallels Haman's — both men mistake the outward appearance of favor for actual security, unaware of the righteous opposition being prepared against them.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 56:8 teaches that 'it is the nature and disposition of almost all men, as soon as they get a little authority, as they suppose, they will immediately begin to exercise unrighteous dominion.' Haman's boasting about his elevation and exclusive access reveals a man intoxicated with the authority he imagines he holds, unaware that it is temporary and conditional.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that true honor and security come not from worldly recognition but from covenants with God. Haman seeks honor from the queen and king; a covenant person seeks honor from God alone.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse foreshadows the way the very mechanism of Christ's apparent defeat — his crucifixion by the Roman authorities — became the mechanism of his exaltation and the salvation of the world. Like Haman, the enemies of Christ thought they were securing their position by eliminating him, not understanding that his apparent destruction was his ultimate victory.
commentary.application: Haman's boasting about his exclusive access to the queen teaches us a humbling truth: we often cannot see the full context of our circumstances. What appears to be a sign of favor may be a setup. What seems like a secure position may be the moment just before a reversal. More importantly, the things we boast about — our special relationships, our unique access, our exclusive privileges — can become sources of danger if they cause us to let down our guard or trust in something fragile. The only secure foundation is covenant relationship with God, not social position, no matter how elevated. Haman's fatal blindness is that he mistakes social honor for actual security. In our own lives, we should ask: What are we counting on for our sense of importance or safety? Is that foundation stable, or is it dependent on the continued favor of others?

text_kjv: Yet all this availeth me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate.

commentary.narrative:
Haman's confession in this verse represents one of the most psychologically penetrating moments in the Hebrew Bible—a man's complete internal collapse. He has just enumerated his wealth, his sons, his promotion above all other princes, and the exclusive favor of Queen Esther herself. By any ordinary measure of success in the ancient Near Eastern court, Haman has achieved everything. Yet all of it—the entire catalog of achievement—registers as worthless to him. The turning point is not abstract philosophy but concrete perception: the moment he sees Mordecai sitting at the king's gate, every treasure becomes ash.

What makes this passage so devastating is that it reveals the fragility of a narcissistic identity structure. Haman's self-worth is not rooted in his actual accomplishments or possessions; it depends entirely on universal submission and deference. One man's refusal to bow—Mordecai's passive resistance—has become the lens through which Haman views his entire life. The Hebrew word shoveh (שׁוֶה), here rendered 'availeth' in the KJV or 'worthless' in The Covenant Rendering, literally means 'equal' or 'sufficient.' Nothing is sufficient. Nothing weighs enough against the burden of Mordecai's defiance.

The phrase 'every time I see Mordecai' (bekhol et asher ani ro'eh) indicates that this is not a fleeting moment of irritation but a recurring torment. Each day Mordecai appears at the gate and refuses to bow, Haman's entire sense of achievement collapses anew. This is the spiritual danger of letting another person's autonomy control your identity: you become enslaved to their presence, to their choices, to their refusal to validate you. Haman has unconsciously made himself Mordecai's prisoner.

word_study.meaning: to be equal, to be sufficient, to be worth; the verb form indicates 'to make equal or equivalent.' In the negative (einennu shoveh), it means 'is not equal to, does not weigh against, is insufficient.' The term carries the sense of not measuring up—something that should balance the scales does not.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering preserves the force of this term better than 'availeth': Haman is saying all his accomplishments are 'not equal' to what his psyche requires—which is total deference from all men. This reveals that his identity crisis is not about objective reality but about an internal standard that can never be satisfied. In covenant terms, this is the opposite of the Latter-day Saint understanding of worth, which is unconditional and rooted in divine sonship, not in others' submission.

word_study.meaning: sitting, dwelling, remaining in a place; present participle suggesting both a state and a continuity. The word emphasizes Mordecai's visible, ongoing presence at the gate.
word_study.significance: The choice of yoshev rather than a dynamic verb (acting, moving, plotting) underscores that Mordecai's mere existence—his refusal to disappear—is what torments Haman. It is not what Mordecai does but simply that he is there, unmoved and immovable. This passive resistance becomes the most powerful force in the narrative.

word_study.meaning: the Jew; the definite article 'ha-' makes this specific and emphatic. It designates Mordecai's ethnic and religious identity, not merely his personal name.
word_study.significance: Haman's reference to Mordecai as 'the Jew' rather than by name is significant: he is defined entirely by his otherness, his refusal to assimilate. For Haman, Mordecai represents not a man but a category—a symbol of defiance against the totalizing power he demands. This hint of antisemitism—reducing a person to an ethnic marker—foreshadows the plot to exterminate an entire people.

cross_references.connection: Mordecai's original refusal to bow to Haman establishes the relational wound that now torments Haman. This verse shows the beginning of the conflict that will consume Haman's mind.

The proverb warns that a prudent man foresees evil and hides, while the foolish pass on and are punished. Haman's inability to see the danger ahead—his blindness to his own impending fall—illustrates foolishness.

Saul's torment when the women praised David more than him offers a parallel portrait of jealous hatred rooted in insecurity. Like Haman, Saul cannot enjoy his position because another's reputation diminishes his.

Zeezrom's pride manifests similarly: external success means nothing because internal peace is lost. The Zoramites' wealth and status do not satisfy their souls because they lack genuine righteousness.

This passage warns that 'the rights of the priesthood are inseparably connected with the powers of heaven,' and that without love, the priesthood becomes a tool of unrighteous dominion. Haman's demand for total submission inverts this principle—he seeks power without love, which eventually consumes him.

commentary.historical_context: In the Persian court, the position Haman holds—grand vizier or chief administrator—would have been one of the highest ranks available to a non-royal. His wealth and his promotion represent the apex of what a subject could achieve under Persian imperial rule. The fact that he has been elevated above all other princes (Esther 3:1) indicates exceptional royal favor. Yet in the ancient Near East, such positions carried inherent insecurity: advancement depended entirely on the king's whim and could be reversed instantly. Haman's anxious obsession with Mordecai's refusal to bow may reflect the precariousness of court life itself. A single gesture of disrespect, if it signals broader dissatisfaction or conspiracy, could undermine a vizier's authority and invite the king's suspicion. The psychological toll of maintaining dominance in such an environment—where your position depends on absolute compliance from subordinates—would have been enormous. Haman's breakdown suggests a man whose entire identity has been constructed on a foundation too narrow to sustain it.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mormon's record of the Nephite civilization, various leaders—Korihor, Alma the Younger before his conversion, even the Zoramites—manifest a similar spiritual disease: the elevation of self above others and the demand for submission. Mormon observes that pride leads to blindness (Helaman 12:1-2). Haman's inability to see his danger parallels the spiritual blindness that precedes the fall of the Nephite kingdoms.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:25-27 describes those who 'received not the testimony of Jesus' and 'denied the Holy Spirit'—the passage emphasizes that such people become focused on their own kingdoms and power. Haman's singular focus on his own glory and Mordecai's refusal to acknowledge it reflects this inward-turning pride that separates from light.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that God's power and authority operate through love and respect for the agency of others, not through coercion. Haman's demand for absolute submission without reciprocal respect inverts the covenant model. His inability to find satisfaction despite outward success illustrates the spiritual poverty of pursuing power divorced from principle.

commentary.christological_typology: While Esther does not explicitly reference Christ, Mordecai's quiet refusal to bow—rooted in religious principle—foreshadows the willingness of believers to refuse worldly submission. Conversely, Haman's obsession with being honored above all others inverts the pattern of Christ, who humbled Himself and sought no honor for Himself (John 5:41). Haman's torment is the inevitable result of building identity on a foundation other than truth. Christ's peace, by contrast, comes from complete alignment with the Father's will.
commentary.application: This verse exposes a painful truth about identity and worth: if your sense of value depends on others' submission to you, you have handed them the power to destroy your peace. Haman has made himself a prisoner to Mordecai's will—not because Mordecai has done anything to him, but because Haman has invested all his self-worth in a single demand: that everyone must acknowledge his superiority. For modern covenant members, this is a crucial warning. We live in an age of social comparison, status-seeking, and the demand for validation. Every time you scroll through social media comparing your achievements to another's, every time you feel diminished because someone else received recognition, every time you feel compelled to prove your worth to people who question it—you are building a Haman-like structure that will eventually collapse. True worth, in LDS theology, is unconditional: you are of infinite worth because you are a child of God, not because of your promotion, your possessions, or anyone's acknowledgment of your superiority. The moment you catch yourself thinking 'all this means nothing because that person will not submit to me,' you have identified an area where you need to release others' agency and rebuild your identity on doctrine, not on dominion.

text_kjv: Then said Zeresh his wife and all his friends unto him, Let a gallows be made of fifty cubits high, and to morrow speak thou unto the king that Mordecai may be hanged thereon: then go thou in merrily with the king unto the banquet. And the thing pleased Haman; and he caused the gallows to be made.

commentary.narrative:
This verse marks a crucial turn toward catastrophe—yet the narrative's genius is that the catastrophe will not be what anyone plans. Zeresh and Haman's friends offer what seems like a logical solution to his torment: remove the obstacle. Kill Mordecai before sunrise, then go to the queen's banquet in good spirits, as if nothing is wrong. The coldness of this advice is striking—they treat murder as casually as removing an inconvenient guest. More tellingly, they promise that Mordecai's death will restore Haman's joy. His misery, they suggest, is situational and remediable: eliminate Mordecai, and the weight will lift.

Haman acts on this counsel immediately. The stakes—rendered as 'gallows' in the KJV but better understood as a tall wooden stake for impalement, as The Covenant Rendering indicates—is constructed to a height of fifty cubits (approximately seventy-five feet). This is no private execution; it is a public spectacle. The structure will be visible across the city of Susa, a monument to Haman's power and Mordecai's punishment. The narrator emphasizes that this is not merely an instrument of execution but a declaration: here is what defiance brings. Haman's intent is to transform his private shame into public validation of his authority.

Yet the narrative contains a hidden irony that the reader begins to perceive. The same night on which Haman builds this instrument of death, the king will lie awake (Esther 6:1), will read from the chronicles, will discover that Mordecai saved his life, and will ask how Mordecai was honored—only to learn he was not. By morning, when Haman comes to ask the king's permission to execute Mordecai, the king's disposition toward him will have shifted. The stakes that Haman builds to kill Mordecai will, by divine Providence (though the name is never spoken), become the instrument of Haman's own death. Haman's confidence that the morning will bring relief from his torment is about to be shattered in the most ironic and devastating way possible.

word_study.meaning: wood, wooden structure, timber; often used for implements of execution. The term is general enough that it could refer to a gallows, cross, stake, or pole. In the context of ancient Persian execution practices, impalement on a stake was a known form of capital punishment, more likely than hanging in the strict sense.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's translation of 'stake' better reflects the likely historical practice than 'gallows.' The word ets appears again at 7:10 when Haman himself is 'hanged' (yitlu) on the ets he prepared. This creates a poetic justice—the instrument Haman builds becomes his own undoing. In Hebrew, the repetition of the same word (ets, yitlu) for both intended and actual execution creates a structural symmetry that suggests divine reversal.

word_study.meaning: high, tall, exalted; used both literally for physical height and metaphorically for pride or honor. The word carries connotations of elevation, prominence, and visibility.
word_study.significance: The choice of gavoah is deliberate: Haman does not want a hidden execution. He wants the stake to be high, visible, a monument to his power and Mordecai's defeat. Yet in Hebrew wisdom literature, gavoah (pride, exaltation) is often the prelude to a fall (Proverbs 16:18, 18:12). The very word used to describe the stake's impressive height subtly hints at the theme of humiliation to come.

word_study.meaning: happy, joyful, glad; the adjective indicates a state of rejoicing. Used both for personal happiness and festive celebration.
word_study.significance: Zeresh's promise is that Mordecai's death will restore sameach—joy—to Haman. She is saying his misery is curable, situational, dependent on external circumstances. Yet joy rooted in another person's death is a false joy, built on a false foundation. The narrative will demonstrate that sameach cannot be sustained by violence; Haman will die without ever experiencing the joy he expected from Mordecai's execution.

word_study.meaning: let them hang, let them impale; causative form of the verb, indicating that one person causes another's execution by hanging or impaling. The same verb appears in Esther 2:23 for the execution of the conspirators who plotted against King Ahasuerus.
word_study.significance: This verb ties Mordecai's intended fate to the conspirators' actual fate, creating a narrative parallel. More importantly, the same verb will be used of Haman's death at 7:10. The repetition of yitlu for both Haman's intended victim and Haman himself creates a linguistic echo that signals reversal and divine justice.

word_study.term_original: יִיטַב הַדָּבָר לִפְנֵי הָמָן (yitav ha-davar lifnei Haman)
word_study.meaning: the thing/matter was good/pleasing before Haman; literally 'the matter was good in Haman's sight.' This phrase indicates approval and satisfaction.
word_study.significance: The narrator's dry observation that 'the idea pleased Haman' marks the moment of Haman's committed choice. He does not hesitate, does not question, does not consider alternatives. He embraces the plan immediately. Yet the reader who knows the ending recognizes this as the moment of his sealing fate. His haste, his certainty, his pleasure in the plan all become ironic markers of his blindness.

cross_references.connection: The very night Haman builds the stake, the king cannot sleep and discovers that Mordecai was never honored. When Haman arrives to ask the king's permission to execute Mordecai, he finds the disposition completely reversed, setting the stage for Haman's own downfall.

Haman is 'hanged' (yitlu) on the very stake (ets) he had prepared for Mordecai. The repetition of these words creates poetic justice: the instrument meant for Mordecai becomes Haman's instrument of death.
This proverb states: 'Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein.' Haman's plan to destroy Mordecai becomes the pit into which Haman himself falls—a classic reversal of intention.
The psalmist describes how the wicked conceive mischief, become pregnant with iniquity, and then bring forth lies—only to fall into the pit they have dug. Haman's arc follows this exact pattern.

Mormon writes that 'the plan of mercy could not be brought about except an atonement should be made.' Here, the plan of destruction cannot be brought about except through the reversal of Haman's own intention—a negative mirror of how divine mercy operates.

This verse teaches forgiveness and warns against vengeance: 'I, the Lord, will forgive whom I will forgive, but of you it is required to forgive all men.' Haman's obsession with vengeance—killing Mordecai—becomes the framework through which his own death is accomplished.

commentary.historical_context: The execution method described—impalement on a stake visible across the city—was indeed practiced in the Persian Empire and in ancient Near Eastern cultures more broadly. Herodotus and other Greek historians describe Persian methods of execution, and impalement was among them. The height of the stake (fifty cubits, approximately seventy-five feet) would have made it visible for considerable distance, ensuring that the execution served not only as punishment but as political theater. In the context of Persian court politics, the public nature of the execution was essential to Haman's purpose: he needed to demonstrate to the entire court that defiance against him had catastrophic consequences. The night-time construction of the stake is historically plausible as well; a vizier with the resources and authority to command such a project could have had it completed quickly. The narrative's emphasis on speed—Zeresh suggests they build it 'tonight' and approach the king 'in the morning'—reflects the urgency of court life, where decisions could be made and executed with startling rapidity. However, what the narrative does not explicitly state but what the reader understands is that between the evening when the stake is built and the morning when Haman plans to approach the king, the entire situation will have changed. The king's sleeplessness and discovery will alter his disposition, making Haman's plan not merely unsuccessful but catastrophically counterproductive.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of Haman's quick confidence followed by swift reversal echoes the Nephite tendency to build destructive plans without perceiving the spiritual forces arrayed against them. Laman and Lemuel's murderous plots against Nephi, the Zoramites' pride before their exposure and humiliation—these all follow the same arc: hasty decision, confident execution, and unexpected reversal.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:22-23 teaches that 'no power or influence can or ought to be maintained by virtue of the priesthood, only by persuasion, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned.' Haman's attempt to maintain power through execution and fear inverts this principle entirely. His method, based on coercion rather than persuasion, is spiritually destined to fail.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that covenants made without integrity—that is, made with intent to harm or deceive—are not valid and cannot be sustained by divine power. Haman's plan, built on deception and murder, is cosmically unstable. The reversal that occurs is not punishment imposed from outside but the natural collapse of a structure built on a false foundation.

commentary.christological_typology: Haman's construction of the instrument of his own death inverts the meaning of the cross in Christian typology. Where Christ's executioners meant His death as defeat and mockery, but it became the instrument of salvation, Haman's executioners (ironically, the king and Haman's own enemies) use his own prepared stake for his destruction. More broadly, the narrative illustrates the principle that those who take up the sword (or in this case, the stake) to destroy others will themselves be destroyed—a principle Christ enunciated to Peter in Matthew 26:52. The reversal also suggests that the instruments of evil cannot ultimately be wielded against the righteous; they turn against their makers.
commentary.application: This verse offers a chilling lesson about the consequences of allowing bitterness and jealousy to drive action. Zeresh's 'practical' advice—kill Mordecai and move on—seems reasonable in the context of her husband's torment. But the narrative reveals that this 'solution' solves nothing and actually accelerates the catastrophe. For modern readers, the lesson is this: when you are in pain or humiliation, the last people whose advice you should follow are those who validate your desire for vengeance. Zeresh does not challenge Haman to examine why one man's existence matters so much to him; she does not encourage him to find meaning apart from universal acclaim; she does not suggest he is destroying himself through obsession. Instead, she offers a shortcut: eliminate the problem person and regain your joy. This is precisely the counsel that destroys Haman. In your own life, when you are tempted to remove someone from your sphere (through rejection, retaliation, or worse) to solve an emotional problem, recognize this moment as dangerous. The people who encourage you toward vengeance may be your closest companions, but they are leading you toward the stake. True healing requires understanding why another person's autonomy has such power over your peace. And that understanding typically cannot come from anyone who shares your bitterness—it can only come from humility, from reflection on why you have made another person's submission essential to your joy.

text_kjv: On that night could not the king sleep, and he commanded to bring the book of records of the chronicles; and they were read before the king.

commentary.narrative: This verse opens the chapter that reverses the entire plot of Esther. The king's insomnia is presented not as a frustration but as the providential catalyst that sets all that follows in motion. Ahasuerus, unable to sleep, orders the royal chronicles brought to his chamber—a commonplace remedy for a royal insomniac, perhaps hoping to bore himself into sleep. Instead, he encounters a written record of Mordecai's loyalty from years earlier (2:21-23), a deed that had been formally documented but apparently forgotten and unrewarded. The passivity of "they were read before the king" suggests the reading process is almost mechanical—the king's servants simply reading entries aloud, with no expectation that anything significant will emerge from the bureaucratic record. Yet within this mundane act lies the mechanism of divine providence working through human institutions. The book of chronicles represents institutional memory, and what had been written in service to the king now serves the king's awareness, triggering the events that will save the Jewish people.

word_study.meaning: The verb nadad (to wander, flee, be restless) personifies sleep as an active entity that departs from the king, rather than the king being unable to sleep. This is a richer image than mere insomnia—sleep itself has abandoned him, suggesting an unsettled state of consciousness.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering captures this nuance well: 'sleep fled from the king' rather than 'the king could not sleep.' The personification suggests something is stirring in the king's mind or spirit, though he does not know what. In the context of providential narrative, this restlessness can be read as divine stirring, the beginning of reversal.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'the book of memorials, the chronicles of days'—the official court record documenting significant events during the king's reign. Zikronot emphasizes memory and record-keeping; yamim (days) indicates a chronological diary or annals.
word_study.significance: This is not casual reading material but the institutional memory of the Persian court. The fact that Mordecai's deed was recorded (2:23) in this very book becomes the pivot point of the story. What was written 'became a matter of record' (2:23) is now discovered at the critical moment. The written word—in a non-scriptural text—becomes an instrument of providence.

word_study.meaning: Passive participle: 'being read, called out.' The passive voice emphasizes that the reading is happening to the king; entries are being presented without his particular direction.
word_study.significance: The passivity is theologically significant. The king is not searching for specific information; the reading simply unfolds, and Mordecai's record is discovered as if by accident. This pattern—divine providence working through ordinary institutional processes—echoes throughout the book of Esther, where God is never mentioned but His hand is everywhere present.

cross_references.connection: This passage records Mordecai's original discovery and report of the assassination plot by Bigthana and Teresh, and notes that the matter was written in the book of chronicles—the very book now being read to the king.
The stake (gallows) that Haman had prepared for Mordecai's execution is already standing, awaiting the king's permission to carry out the death sentence.

The heart of the king is in the Lord's hand, and He turns it as the rivers of water—the king's sleeplessness and his subsequent actions reflect divine direction working through natural human experience.
The pattern of hidden things being brought to light and eternal records being witnessed reflects the principle that all deeds are recorded and will be brought forth, even those long forgotten.

commentary.historical_context: The practice of reading royal chronicles aloud to the king—particularly as a remedy for insomnia or as evening entertainment—is attested in ancient Near Eastern royal courts. Ahasuerus' sleeplessness and his summoning of official records to distract himself reflects the lifestyle and preoccupations of a Persian monarch. The book of records mentioned here parallels the official royal inscriptions and administrative records of the Achaemenid Empire, where detailed chronicles of the reign were maintained. The very fact that Mordecai's deed was formally documented speaks to the Persian bureaucratic tradition of thorough record-keeping. For an ancient audience, the irony would have been profound: the king seeks distraction in dull administrative records and instead discovers information that reverses the political landscape entirely. The reading process itself—a servant reading entries aloud—indicates the formal nature of the chronicles and the king's expectation of passive reception of information.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of hidden deeds coming to light appears in the Book of Mormon when secret records and hidden plans are revealed (Alma 12:3). The principle that God works through institutional memory and written records—not just through miraculous intervention—reflects the Restoration emphasis on word, record, and testimony being central to divine work.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-5 emphasizes that the Lord will preserve records and works for His purposes. The principle of institutional memory serving divine purposes reflects Doctrine and Covenants teaching on the significance of record-keeping and documentation in the Lord's work.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The reading of records parallels the temple emphasis on remembrance and the recording of covenants and deeds. The idea that what is written is preserved and has eternal significance resonates with temple theology concerning the binding nature of recorded covenants.

commentary.christological_typology: While not a direct type of Christ, this verse illustrates the principle that divine providence works through human institutions and records. The hidden record of faithfulness that becomes manifest reflects the pattern of Christ's life and work being recorded and preserved for later revelation and vindication. The reversal pattern—where something long overlooked becomes the key to salvation—prefigures Christ's resurrection and vindication after the apparent defeat of the Cross.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that faithfulness, even when overlooked or forgotten by human observers, is recorded and does not go unnoticed by God. For modern members, it is a reminder that our deeds and integrity are written in a record that matters eternally. The verse also demonstrates that divine providence often works through ordinary human institutions—records, laws, routines—rather than only through miraculous intervention. We should trust that the Lord can use even mundane administrative processes for His purposes. Practically, this invites us to maintain integrity in our dealings even when no one is watching, knowing that the Lord sees and remembers.

text_kjv: And it was found written, that Mordecai had told of Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king's chamberlains, the keepers of the door, who sought to lay hand on the king Ahasuerus.

commentary.narrative: The reader—or the king himself—discovers in the chronicles the written account of Mordecai's report of an assassination plot. This is not new information to the narrative (the reader learned it in 2:21-23), but it is new information to the king at this critical moment. The phrase "it was found written" emphasizes the act of discovery; the entry was always there, but its rediscovery at this precise hour is what gives it power. The conspiracy involved two eunuchs, Bigthana and Teresh, who were threshold guards—men with access to the king's person and therefore in position to strike. The phrase "sought to lay hand on the king" is an idiom for assassination, conveying the directness of the threat. What is remarkable is that this threat was thwarted by Mordecai's vigilance, and yet years have passed without the king acknowledging or rewarding the man who saved his life. This oversight is about to become the hinge upon which the entire reversal turns. The written record serves as testimony to a debt unpaid.

word_study.meaning: Passive construction: 'it was found written/recorded.' The verb matsa (to find) emphasizes discovery; katuv (written) suggests the permanence and authority of the written record.
word_study.significance: The passive voice—'it was found'—maintains the narrative ambiguity about whether this is chance or providence. The Covenant Rendering's 'it was found recorded' captures the sense that the writing itself is the vehicle of discovery. The deed was written (2:23) and is now found; the written word is the means by which past faithfulness becomes present leverage.

word_study.meaning: Hiphil form of nagad: to tell, report, make known. This is the same verb used in 2:21 for Mordecai's initial report of the conspiracy.
word_study.significance: The repetition of language from 2:21 reinforces continuity: Mordecai's original act of loyalty is being referenced in the exact terms in which it was documented. The verb higgid also carries a sense of bearing witness or making manifest—Mordecai brought the hidden threat into the light.

word_study.meaning: Sarisei (eunuchs, chamberlains) and shomerei ha-saf (guards of the threshold/door). These men were in the most intimate positions of power in the court—gatekeepers with access to the king.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that these were 'two of the king's eunuchs from the threshold guards.' Their position made them uniquely dangerous; they could approach the king. The fact that they could be stopped by Mordecai's alertness reveals that vigilance—paying attention—is a form of power in the court.

word_study.meaning: The phrase 'to send a hand' is an ancient idiom for assassination or violent attack. The verb biqesh (to seek, attempt) indicates intention and effort toward harm.
word_study.significance: This is not a minor breach of protocol but an attempt on the king's life. The preservation of the king's life is therefore a significant service, one that a king—especially an Eastern despot—would be expected to repay generously.

cross_references.connection: The original account of Mordecai's discovery of the conspiracy and the explicit note that the matter was written in the chronicles forms the background for this verse's discovery.

Mordecai's refusal to bow to Haman is the trigger for Haman's plot against the Jews; yet Mordecai's earlier loyalty to the king remains the ultimate counterweight that will save both Mordecai and the Jews.
The psalmist laments that his good deeds are returned with hatred; Mordecai's experience parallels this pattern until the moment of this verse's discovery.

David's similar pattern of saving the life of Nabal indirectly, only to be rewarded in due time through divine intervention, reflects the broader biblical pattern of faithfulness being eventually acknowledged.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Persian court tradition, the threshold guards (saf in Hebrew, cognate to Persian 'darvazband') were highly trusted officials responsible for controlling access to the king's person. They were frequently eunuchs, as were many court attendants in ancient Near Eastern royal courts. The conspiracy itself reflects the real dangers faced by Eastern monarchs; assassination plots by court insiders are documented in Persian sources. The practice of maintaining detailed chronicles of such incidents would have been standard in the Achaemenid court. The fact that the conspiracy was discovered and documented—and that Mordecai was credited—indicates both the seriousness with which the Persian court took such threats and the bureaucratic precision with which they recorded them. For a Persian audience, the detail about Bigthana and Teresh being eunuchs and threshold guards would have conveyed the gravity of the threat: these were men with intimate access to the king's chambers.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon emphasizes the principle that faithfulness is recorded and witnessed. Alma 37:8-9 teaches that small things lead to great things; Mordecai's small act of reporting the conspiracy becomes the mechanism for the salvation of his people.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:40 teaches that all things are spiritual and visible before God; nothing is hidden from Him. The written record in the chronicles parallels the principle that all deeds are recorded in a heavenly record.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony emphasizes the recording of covenants and the eternal significance of recorded transactions. The written chronicle serves a similar function in the Persian court: it preserves the record of a covenantal obligation (the king owes gratitude to Mordecai for saving his life).

commentary.christological_typology: Mordecai's hidden faithfulness, long unacknowledged, being recorded and brought to light reflects the pattern of hidden righteousness being made manifest. The preservation of Mordecai's name in the written record—like the preservation of names in the Lamb's book of life—suggests that faithful deeds are never truly hidden from the record that matters eternally.
commentary.application: This verse reinforces that our faithfulness is recorded, not merely in earthly chronicles but in the divine record. Even when our good works are unnoticed or unrewarded by others, they are written down in the account that God keeps. Modern members are invited to serve faithfully without expectation of immediate recognition, trusting that the Lord records and eventually acknowledges all faithful service. The verse also teaches discernment and courage: Mordecai's willingness to report a conspiracy against the king, even though it placed him in a position to make dangerous enemies, was an act of integrity. We are called to similar moral courage in speaking truth even when it may not be immediately rewarded.

text_kjv: And the king said, What honour and dignity hath been done to Mordecai for this? Then said the king's servants that ministered unto him, There is nothing done for him.

commentary.narrative: Upon reading the account of Mordecai's loyalty, the king's first response is to ask what reward has been given. This question reveals the king's sense of proper protocol: a subject who saves the king's life deserves recognition and honor. The king's question is direct and assumes that something has been done—he asks "what honor and dignity has been done to Mordecai for this?" The servants' response is blunt and devastating: nothing has been done. This is not a partial or delayed reward; it is complete oversight. The fact that the king's attendants must answer this question (rather than the king already knowing) indicates that Mordecai's service had been officially forgotten despite being formally recorded. This represents a serious administrative failure, a breach of the unwritten law of reciprocal obligation that governed ancient Near Eastern courts. For a king to fail to honor someone who had saved his life was shameful and problematic, not only for the subject deprived of reward but for the king's own honor and credibility. The king's reaction to this oversight will become the mechanism by which Mordecai receives not just recognition but elevation.

word_study.meaning: Yeqar denotes honor, esteem, weight (literal and figurative); gedulah denotes greatness, magnificence, dignity. Together they form a hendiadys expressing supreme honor.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering simplifies to 'honor or recognition,' but the Hebrew pairing of yeqar (personal honor) and gedulah (political greatness) suggests both personal recognition and public elevation. These are the very terms that will characterize the honor the king ultimately gives Mordecai in verse 11.

word_study.meaning: Passive perfect: 'has been done, has been made.' The passive voice places focus on the action of honoring, regardless of who performed it.
word_study.significance: The verb's passive form suggests the king is asking about an action that should have occurred as a matter of protocol. That it has not occurred is the problem.

word_study.meaning: Thing, word, matter. In this negative construction ('nothing') it is comprehensive—not even a small thing, not even a token acknowledgment.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's translation 'nothing has been done for him' captures the totality of the oversight. The word davar often carries weight in biblical usage; here its negation is emphatic. No reward, no public acknowledgment, no elevation whatsoever.

word_study.term_english: the king's servants that ministered unto him
word_study.meaning: Na'arim (young men, servants) and mesharim (those who minister, serve). These are the attendants in close service to the king.
word_study.significance: These are the king's intimate advisors and servants—people who would know the state of rewards and honors given by the king. Their answer carries authority.

cross_references.connection: The honor the king ultimately grants Mordecai—parading him through the city in royal garb—far exceeds any ordinary reward and becomes the centerpiece of the reversal.
A person diligent in their work shall stand before kings; Mordecai's alertness and loyalty position him to receive the king's favor.
The concern for honor before the elders and people reflects ancient Near Eastern protocol: a king's failure to honor a benefactor was a public failure.
The principle that the Lord expects those in authority to give to those in need and to acknowledge faithful service reflects the same protocol principle at work here.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Persian court culture, the concept of reciprocal obligation was fundamental. A benefactor—especially one who saved the king's life—had a claim on the king's gratitude that extended beyond mere thanks; it typically demanded public recognition and material reward. The failure to honor such a beneficiary was not merely an individual oversight but a breach of court protocol that reflected poorly on the king's judgment and honor. The servants' ability to answer definitively that nothing had been done suggests that honor and rewards were systematically tracked and publicly known. The astonishment that nothing had been done for Mordecai indicates that such a service would normally trigger an immediate and substantial reward. The fact that it had been entirely overlooked, despite being recorded, speaks to either the king's absent-mindedness or the marginalization of Mordecai (perhaps as a non-Persian or lower-status official). The bureaucratic nature of the Persian court—evidenced by the keeping of detailed chronicles—meant that administrative oversights were precisely what could happen: a record existed, but the protocol for responding to that record had failed.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 26:27 emphasizes that the Lord is aware of the works of his people; even when overlooked by mortals, faithful service is recorded. The pattern of Mordecai being overlooked until the record is read parallels the pattern of the righteous being elevated at God's appointed time.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:41-43 teaches that the powers of heaven can only be wielded by righteousness and gentle persuasion; the king's authority to elevate Mordecai is itself contingent on responding appropriately to the record of faithfulness brought before him.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple emphasis on the recording of covenants and the obligation to honor covenantal commitments parallels the king's obligation here. The king's realization that he has a debt to Mordecai mirrors the awakening to covenantal obligation.

commentary.christological_typology: The king's realization that someone has saved his life and deserves honor reflects the reality of Christ's atonement: the Son of God has done something infinite and unspeakable to redeem mankind, and this deed demands appropriate response and gratitude. The pattern of hidden faithfulness being brought to light and then honored prefigures the revelation of Christ's work and the eternal recognition that will attend it.
commentary.application: This verse addresses the anxiety many feel about being overlooked or unrewarded for their faithful service. Mordecai's situation teaches that earthly recognition may be delayed or overlooked by those in authority, but the record remains. The verse also invites those in positions of leadership or influence to examine their accountability: we are responsible for acknowledging and honoring faithful service, both because it is just and because it reflects our own integrity. Practically, members should examine whether they are overlooking or taking for granted the faithful service of others—spouses, family members, friends, fellow church members—and move to offer genuine recognition and honor.

text_kjv: And the king said, Who is in the court? Now Haman was come into the outward court of the king's house, to speak unto the king to hang Mordecai on the gallows that he had prepared for him.

commentary.narrative: This verse contains the central irony of chapter 6: the precise moment when the king asks for advice on how to honor Mordecai, Haman arrives in the court with the intention of requesting Mordecai's execution. The verse is structured to emphasize the simultaneity and the complete mutual incomprehension of the two men's purposes. The king asks casually, "Who is in the court?"—a simple request for whoever is available to give counsel. The narrator then informs the reader that Haman has just arrived at the outer court for an entirely different purpose: to obtain the king's permission to execute Mordecai on the gallows (or stake) he had prepared in 5:14. Neither man knows what the other is about to propose. From Haman's perspective, his timing is perfect: he is arriving to finalize the destruction of his enemy, and he has the king's attention. From the king's perspective, the moment is providential—help has arrived in the form of the first available courtier. From the reader's perspective, the irony is devastating. Haman is walking into a trap laid not by Mordecai or by human conspiracy, but by the pattern of consequences that his own actions have set in motion. The stake he built becomes the instrument of his own destruction.

word_study.meaning: A simple interrogative: 'who' (mi), 'in' (be), 'the court/courtyard' (chatser). The chatser is the outer courtyard where courtiers and officials wait.
word_study.significance: The casualness of the king's question is the literary engine of the irony. He has no particular person in mind; he simply asks for whoever is available. The question presupposes that someone suitable will be present.

word_study.term_english: had come into the outer court
word_study.meaning: Ba (to come, arrive); chatsar (courtyard); beit ha-melekh (the king's house); chitsonah (outer, external). The phrase specifies the outer courtyard—the formal space where official courtiers present themselves.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'outer court of the king's palace' clarifies the spatial hierarchy: Haman has not yet entered the inner chambers where the king is; he is waiting in the formal receiving area. This detail matters because it will be the servants who summon him into the king's presence.

word_study.term_english: to speak unto the king to hang
word_study.term_original: לְהָבִ֞יא אֶת־סֵ֤פֶר הַזִּכְרֹנוֹת֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י הַיָּמִ֔ים וַיִּהְי֥וּ נִקְרָאִ֖ים לִפְנֵ֥י הַמֶּֽלֶךְ
word_study.meaning: Le'emor (to say, speak); litlot (to hang, impale, crucify); the infinitive construction indicates purpose or intention.
word_study.significance: Haman's arrival in the court is explicitly for the purpose of 'asking the king to have Mordecai impaled' (Covenant Rendering). The word litlot (to hang) is the same word that will describe Haman's own fate in 7:10. The repetition creates a grim verbal irony: Haman is coming to request the execution method that will be used on himself.

word_study.term_english: the stake he had prepared for him
word_study.meaning: Etz (tree, wood, stake, gallows); hekin (to prepare, make ready, establish). The stake has been prepared in advance of the king's permission to use it.
word_study.significance: Haman's presumption is evident in the fact that he has already built the instrument of execution. He is coming to the king to formalize what he apparently considers a foregone conclusion. This presumption will contribute to his undoing; he has committed resources and effort to a plan that depends entirely on the king's cooperation.

cross_references.connection: Zeresh and Haman's friends had counseled him to build the gallows fifty cubits high and speak to the king in the morning about hanging Mordecai; Haman has followed this advice, and now comes to execute it.
The ironic outcome: Mordecai will not be hanged on the stake, but Haman himself will be impaled on the very stake he prepared.
He that diggeth a pit shall fall therein; Haman's careful preparation of the means of execution becomes his own undoing.
He made a pit, and digged it, and is fallen into the ditch which he made; the pattern of the wicked preparing destruction for themselves.
The principle that all things work together for the salvation of the righteous and the condemnation of the wicked reflects the pattern at work here.

commentary.historical_context: The Persian court protocol, as reflected in the text, involved multiple courtyards and chambers with increasingly restricted access. The outer courtyard (chatsar ha-chitsonah) was the formal receiving area where officials and petitioners would wait for an audience. The king's private chambers would have been in the inner sanctum. The custom of courtiers waiting in the outer court for the king's summons reflects actual Persian court procedure. The phrase 'to speak unto the king' (le'emor la-melekh) indicates a formal petition—Haman is not going to whisper suggestions but to make an official request. The fact that Haman has prepared the gallows in advance reflects both his confidence in his position and the Persian practice of capital punishment for those found guilty of sedition or serious crime. The height of the gallows (fifty cubits, as mentioned in 5:14) was designed to be publicly visible, increasing the shame and horror of the execution.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:20-21 teaches that guilt and remorse come upon those who persist in wickedness; Haman's confident approach to the throne contrasts with the fate awaiting him. The Nephites' experience of seeing their enemies fall into pits they had prepared for others (Alma 48:24-25) parallels Haman's fate.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 109:46 teaches that the Lord will chasten the nations but deliver the righteous; the pattern of Haman's plot rebounding on himself while Mordecai is preserved illustrates this principle.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple emphasis on the justice and mercy of God—that He will not allow the wicked to triumph over the righteous indefinitely—is at work in this verse. The timing of Haman's arrival as the king is asking for advice on honoring Mordecai suggests that divine ordering extends even to the precise moment.

commentary.christological_typology: The ironic structure of this verse—where the instrument of death becomes the means of salvation—prefigures the central paradox of the cross. What Haman meant for evil and what he designed for execution becomes instead the occasion of reversal and salvation. The pattern of human pride and plotting being overturned by divine providence reflects the ultimate overturning of Satan's designs through Christ's atonement.
commentary.application: This verse invites reflection on the nature of Providence and the limits of human planning. Haman's careful schemes, his advance preparation, his timing—all prove futile not because they are opposed by a mightier human conspiracy but because they are contrary to the larger pattern of justice and mercy that governs the cosmos. Modern members are invited to trust that their own faithful service and righteous living are woven into a larger pattern that God oversees. It also challenges those prone to fear powerful enemies: Haman's confidence and preparation do not save him. More practically, the verse warns against presumption in evil: planning someone's harm, even with care and advance preparation, can become the instrument of one's own undoing. The believer's responsibility is to trust Providence rather than to fear human power, and to refrain from plans of harm against others.

text_kjv: And the king's servants said unto him, Behold, Haman standeth in the court. And the king said, Let him come in.

commentary.narrative: The verse is brief and direct: the king's servants report that Haman is waiting in the courtyard, and the king immediately invites him in. This brevity serves the narrative perfectly. There is no hesitation, no question, no awareness of anything other than the convenient fact that someone suitable has appeared at the moment needed. The servants' simple announcement—"Haman is standing in the court"—conveys no sense of drama or significance. They are simply reporting his presence. The king's equally simple response—"Let him come in"—grants permission for Haman to enter the royal presence. For Haman, this represents the moment of triumph: he has been granted the king's attention and is about to make his request for Mordecai's execution. For the king, this represents the answer to a bureaucratic need: advice on how to honor Mordecai. For the reader, this verse is the nadir of suspense before the reversal is complete. Everything now depends on what Haman does when he enters the king's chamber. He will be asked for advice on honoring someone, and his answer—born of arrogance and presumption—will become the mechanism of his own destruction. The simplicity of the verse masks the complexity of the irony about to unfold.

word_study.meaning: An exclamatory particle: 'look, behold.' It draws attention to what follows.
word_study.significance: The word conveys immediacy and presence: Haman is here, now, standing in the court. The servants are simply directing the king's attention to a present fact.

word_study.meaning: Participle of amad: 'standing.' The participle indicates a ongoing state or position.
word_study.significance: Haman is standing and waiting—in a position of subordination relative to the king, yet poised to make his request. The word suggests formal readiness.

word_study.meaning: Cohortative form: 'let him go in, come in.' The king's permission granted.
word_study.significance: The brevity of the king's response is significant. There is no consultation, no hesitation, no inquiry. The king simply grants access, which is his prerogative but also his potential vulnerability: he is about to be counseled by someone with hidden motives.

cross_references.connection: When Haman's treachery is revealed, the king will command that Haman be impaled on the very stake he prepared, and one of the eunuchs will report that it is already standing in Haman's house.
Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall; Haman's confidence in his favorable standing with the king leads directly to his undoing.
The contrast between human plans and divine purposes: Haman plans one thing, but the course of events will be determined by forces beyond his control.
The principle that the wicked cannot comprehend the thoughts of the righteous or the purposes of the Lord reflects Haman's fundamental misreading of the situation.

commentary.historical_context: The protocol of court access—in which a king could grant or deny an audience to courtiers waiting in the outer chamber—reflects actual Persian administrative practice. The eunuchs or servants who conveyed messages and controlled access were themselves important figures in the court hierarchy. The fact that the king simply grants access suggests both his absolute authority (he need not justify or question) and his openness to the counsel of his courtiers. In the context of Persian court life, such access would have been eagerly sought and carefully managed. Haman's presence in the court, apparently at the right time to be summoned, suggests both his high status and his frequent access to the king—which makes his fate all the more remarkable.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of the wicked being brought into the presence of judgment appears in Alma 12:14-15, where the Lord brings all secret things to light. Haman is literally brought into the presence where his counseling will expose his true heart and intentions.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:35-36 teaches that any attempt to coerce or control others through unrighteous dominion will eventually be revealed and condemned. Haman's attempt to use his standing with the king will be exposed through his own counsel.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple emphasis on being brought before God for judgment is foreshadowed in Haman's summons to the king's presence, where he will be judged and his true nature revealed.

commentary.christological_typology: The summoning of Haman before the king to be confronted with truth and judged for his schemes prefigures the pattern of judgment where all will be brought before God to account for their deeds. The irony of being summoned expecting favor while facing condemnation reflects the final judgment pattern.
commentary.application: This brief verse teaches the importance of humility and self-awareness. Haman is about to enter a situation he completely misreads because he cannot imagine that his plans might fail or that the king might have purposes other than those he assumes. For modern members, this is an invitation to recognize the limits of our own perception and planning. We may believe our strategies are foolproof or that we understand a situation completely, when in fact we are about to encounter truths that will completely reverse our understanding. The verse also suggests that divine purposes can work through the most ordinary and simple moments: a king asking for advice, a courtier being brought into the royal presence. We should not despise the small, ordinary moments; they may be the hinges on which Providence turns.

text_kjv: So Haman came in. And the king said unto him, What shall be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour? Now Haman thought in his heart, To whom would the king delight to do honour more than to myself?

commentary.narrative: This verse contains the narrative pivot of the entire book of Esther. Haman enters the king's presence, and the king asks him: "What should be done for the man the king wishes to honor?" The king has deliberately obscured the identity of the honoree, asking Haman for his counsel on how to bestow honor without revealing to whom it will be given. This vagueness is either an accident of the king's wording or a narrative device that sets up the irony; either way, it creates a space where Haman's arrogance fills the void. The narrator then grants the reader access to Haman's internal response: "Haman thought in his heart, 'To whom would the king wish to honor more than me?'" The phrase "in his heart" (belibbo) indicates that this is Haman's silent assumption, not spoken but absolute in his mind. Haman's assumption is that the king's favor—and any honor the king wishes to bestow—would naturally be directed toward him. It does not occur to him that anyone else could be the object of the king's desire to honor. This is the fundamental error of Haman's understanding. His arrogance has blinded him to any possibility other than his own elevation. When he responds with suggestions for honoring someone, he will be describing the honors he wishes for himself, not realizing that he is describing the honors that will instead be lavished on his mortal enemy. The verse is the apex of dramatic irony in the book.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'what to be done'; an interrogative with an infinitive construct. The king is asking for a course of action or suggestion.
word_study.significance: The king's question is deliberately framed without specifying the identity of the person to be honored. This open-endedness is what allows Haman to project his own assumptions into the silence.

word_study.term_english: the man whom the king delighteth to honour
word_study.meaning: The phrase 'the man in whom the king delights to honor' uses the construct chafets be- ('takes pleasure in, delights in') with yiqar ('honor, dignity'). The king delights in honoring someone, but has not identified whom.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering captures the ambiguity: 'the man the king wishes to honor.' This vagueness is crucial to the irony. The king knows he means Mordecai, but Haman does not, and his response reveals what he would choose for himself.

word_study.meaning: The phrase 'said in his heart' is an idiom for internal thought or silent assumption. Belibbo ('in his heart') indicates the seat of intention and desire.
word_study.significance: The narrator is granting the reader access to what Haman does not speak aloud but assumes absolutely. This is a device of dramatic irony: we know what Haman is thinking, and we know how wrong his assumption is.

word_study.term_english: To whom would the king delight
word_study.meaning: Mi ('whom'); yachpots (to delight in, take pleasure in, desire). The verb echoes the king's earlier use of chafets: the king delights to honor, and Haman assumes the king would delight to honor him.
word_study.significance: The repetition of the root chafets (to delight, desire) creates a verbal connection: the king's desire to honor and Haman's assumption about the king's desires are expressed in the same terms, but they refer to entirely different people.

word_study.meaning: Yoter means 'more'; mimmenni means 'than me.' The phrase expresses Haman's assumption of his own primacy in the king's favor.
word_study.significance: This phrase reveals the totality of Haman's self-absorption. It does not cross his mind that the king might wish to honor someone other than himself; he simply wonders whether the king might wish to honor someone else MORE. The possibility that the king's favorite is not Haman at all is unthinkable to him.

cross_references.connection: Haman's description of the honor—royal garb, royal horse, proclamation through the streets—becomes the exact honor that is bestowed, but on Mordecai instead of himself.
Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall; Haman's pride in assuming the king's favor is the immediate cause of his downfall.

Samuel's rebuke of Saul: though thou wast little in thine own sight, thou wast made the head of the tribes of Israel; Haman's opposite error—making himself great in his own sight—leads to his condemnation.
The prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself; Haman's failure to foresee the possibility of his own destruction parallels the fool's blindness.
The principle that God is aware of all things and nothing is hidden from Him contrasts with Haman's blindness to the true situation unfolding before him.

commentary.historical_context: The Persian court world is reflected in Haman's assumptions: a man of high rank and favor with the king would have natural expectations of continued elevation and honor. Haman's position as grand vizier would have made him accustomed to the deference of others and to the assumption that the king valued his counsel above all others. The practice of honoring a favored courtier with royal garb, a royal mount, and a public procession was attested in ancient Near Eastern court practice as a means of marking status and favor. For Haman to assume that any honor the king wished to give would be directed toward him reflects not only arrogance but also the conventional patterns of court life: the king's chief counselor would naturally be among the most honored. However, this conventional assumption blinds Haman to the actual situation unfolding.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 12:3-4 teaches that the Lord cannot be deceived and knows the hearts of all people. Haman's attempt to manipulate the situation and his assumption about the king's intentions are exposed precisely because the truth cannot be hidden. Mormon 3:18-19 similarly teaches that pride and self-seeking lead to destruction.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:39 warns against coveting what is not one's own and using power to promote pride and vainglory; Haman's fundamental error is assuming that all honor and favor naturally flows to him. D&C 76:75-80 describes the fate of those who place themselves above others and seek their own exaltation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple emphasis on humility before God and the danger of pride reflects the principle at work here. Haman's assumption that he is the center of the king's attention parallels the spiritual error of those who place themselves rather than God at the center of their universe.

commentary.christological_typology: Haman's blindness to the true nature of the situation—his assumption that he knows the king's intentions when in fact he does not—reflects the spiritual blindness of those who reject Christ. His elaborate plans for his own honor become instead instruments of his own judgment and condemnation. The pattern of the wicked creating instruments of judgment for themselves, only to fall into them, is a recurring pattern in scripture that finds its ultimate antitype in Satan's schemes being turned against him by Christ.
commentary.application: This verse stands as a profound meditation on the danger of arrogance and self-deception. Haman's fatal error is not his scheming or his wickedness (though those are present) but his inability to imagine that he could be wrong about the king's favor. He has built his entire understanding of reality on an assumption—that he is the object of the king's affection—and this assumption blinds him to the actual truth. For modern readers, this is an invitation to examine our own assumptions, particularly those we hold most confidently about ourselves and our status. We may be blind to realities that will soon be manifest. The verse also teaches that one's own proposals will come back to haunt us if we are not speaking truth but projecting our desires onto others. Haman suggests honors that reveal what he wants; those honors then become the standard by which he is judged when his true nature is exposed. More broadly, the verse invites us to cultivate genuine humility—to recognize that we may not understand the full picture, that the king (or God) may have purposes and affections that differ from what we assume, and that arrogance about our own status is a guarantee of downfall.

text_kjv: And Haman answered the king, For the man whom the king delighteth to honour,

commentary.narrative:
Haman, called into the king's presence at dawn, is asked a critical question: what should be done for a man the king wishes to honor? Haman, imagining the question refers to himself, launches into an elaborate prescription for honor. The irony begins here—Haman repeats the king's exact phrasing ("the man whom the king delighteth to honour") before describing what he believes will be his own ceremony. This is a masterclass in dramatic irony: the reader knows Mordecai sits at the king's gate, but Haman assumes the honor is meant for him.

Haman's response reveals the depth of his narcissism. Rather than offering a simple answer, he provides a detailed formula for honoring someone, each element reflecting what he personally desires. The TCR translation notes that Haman "echoes the king's exact phrase" before launching into "his detailed prescription"—he is designing what he believes will be his own honor ceremony. His hesitation, his careful phrasing, his enumeration of specifics—all suggest a man who has fantasized about this moment extensively and is now presenting his fantasy as the answer to the king's question.

word_study.meaning: wishes to honor, delights in honor; chafets is a volitional verb expressing the king's desire or pleasure, while qar (from which qaro, 'honor,' derives) refers to weight, heaviness, and therefore dignity, glory, or weightiness. To honor someone is to give them 'weight' in the eyes of others.
word_study.significance: Haman repeats this exact phrase four times in his response (verses 7-9), but the phrase takes on increasingly desperate meaning as he prescribes his own humiliation. The repetition, which seemed confident when Haman first spoke, becomes ironic—he is describing how his enemy will be honored in his own words.

word_study.meaning: he said, he answered; the simple past narrative form, though here it carries a sense of response or answer to the king's implicit question.
word_study.significance: Haman does not hesitate or deflect. He answers immediately, showing either supreme confidence or the reflexive pride that makes him speak without thinking through the implications of his words.

cross_references.connection: Haman's earlier elevation and Mordecai's earlier refusal to bow establish the rivalry that makes Haman's fantasy of universal honor so psychologically urgent.
"When pride cometh, then cometh shame: but with the lowly is wisdom." Haman's pride in this moment is about to produce the shame he sought to impose on others.
"Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall." Haman's elaborate answer reveals the very pride that will lead to his downfall.

commentary.historical_context: In Persian court culture, the king's favor was the ultimate currency of power and survival. Haman, as vizier, would have been familiar with the elaborate ceremonies by which the Achaemenid court honored distinguished men. The details he describes—royal robes, royal horses, public proclamations—reflect actual Persian court practices. Ancient Near Eastern monarchies used public ceremonies of honor to reinforce the political hierarchy and demonstrate the king's will. Haman's mistake is not in his knowledge of protocol but in his assumption about whom the honor is meant to serve.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of the prideful revealing their own undoing appears in the Book of Mormon when the proud are given 'according to their desires' (Alma 29:4)—Haman's detailed prescription becomes the instrument of his own shame, not his glory.
